UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                             BEFORE THE
               FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION



SOUTHWEST POWER POOL, INC.                              |                     DOCKET NO. ER26-1323-000


                 MOTION TO INTERVENE AND COMMENTS OF
                 ASSOCIATED ELECTRIC COOPERATIVE, INC.

         Associated Electric Cooperative, Inc. (“AECI”) hereby moves to intervene and submits

comments1 seeking clarification of the February 10, 2026, filing submitted by Southwest Power

Pool Inc. (“SPP”)2 to revise the SPP Open Access Transmission Tariff (“Tariff”) 3 to add a

proposed Conditional High Impact Large Load Service (“CHILLS”) that will allow High Impact

Large Loads (“HILLs”) to be served with non-firm conditional transmission service. AECI is

concerned with the lack of transparency by SPP in the CHILLS Filing regarding the impact of

CHILLS on Affected Systems,4 coordination between SPP and Affected System Operators such

as AECI in the CHILLS interconnection study process, and the practical implication of the

proposed curtailment procedures to be used by SPP in connection with CHILLS.

    I.      MOTION TO INTERVENE

         AECI is a rural electric generation and transmission cooperative that is owned by and

provides wholesale power to six regional generation and transmission cooperatives. These regional

generation and transmission cooperatives supply wholesale power to fifty-one distribution

cooperatives in Missouri, three distribution cooperatives in southeast Iowa, and nine distribution

cooperatives in northeast Oklahoma, serving approximately two million members behind roughly

935,000 meters, including homes, farms, schools, businesses and industries. AECI provides

transmission service via an open access transmission tariff over its and its owners’ transmission

systems. AECI is an unregulated transmission utility as that term is defined in the Federal Power

Act, 16 U.S.C. § 824j-l (2024).

         AECI is an Affected System transmission owner with facilities interconnected to the SPP

transmission system. As an Affected System transmission owner that may be materially impacted

by the interconnection of conditional large loads within SPP, AECI has a direct and substantial

interest in the outcome of this proceeding that cannot be adequately represented by any other

participant. Accordingly, AECI respectfully requests that the Commission grant it full party status

in this proceeding.

   II.      COMMUNICATIONS

         Please direct all communications to the persons identified below:

    III.        COMMENTS

           AECI supports SPP’s efforts to develop transmission service options to accommodate new

and emerging large loads, including data-center and Artificial Intelligence (“AI”)-driven loads.

However, AECI is concerned that certain elements of SPP’s CHILLS proposal lack sufficient

detail. AECI is specifically concerned with SPP’s failure to provide details concerning how it plans

to coordinate with Affected System Owners during the CHILLS interconnection process and the

minimal detail SPP provided regarding the mechanics of curtailing HILLs served with non-firm

conditional transmission service. AECI therefore submits these comments to gain clarity of SPP’s

CHILLS implementation plans in the hope that doing so at this early stage will reduce future

uncertainty for interconnected transmission owners, customers, and system operators.

           A.     SPP Should Clarify How It Intends to Follow the Affected System Study
                  Process for the Interconnection of Conditional High Impact Large Loads.

           Given the potential impact of CHILLS on neighboring transmission systems, SPP should

clarify how it intends to follow the Affected System Study processes when studying requests for

CHILLS. The AECI transmission system shares seams with other neighboring transmission

systems, including SPP, Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc. (“MISO”), and

Tennessee Valley Authority (“TVA”). SPP, MISO, and TVA are therefore Affected Systems,

which FERC has defined as electric systems other than the Transmission Provider’s Transmission

System that may be affected by the proposed interconnection of a generating facility. 5 As Affected

Systems, AECI coordinates with SPP, MISO, and TVA when AECI determines that the


5
    See Standardization of Generator Interconnection Agreements and Procedures, 104 FERC ¶ 61,103, at n.32
    (2003) (“Order No. 2003”), order on reh'g, Order No. 2003-A, 106 FERC ¶ 61,220, order on reh'g, Order No.
    2003-B, 109 FERC ¶ 61,287 (2004), order on reh'g, Order No. 2003-C, 111 FERC ¶ 61,301 (2005); aff’d sub
    nom. Nat’l Ass’n of Regul. Util. Comm’rs v. FERC, 475 F.3d 1277 (D.C. Cir. 2007); Reform of Generator
    Interconnection Procedures and Agreements, 157 FERC ¶ 61,212, at n.198 (2016).
 Docket No. ER26-1323-000

interconnection of a generating facility on its transmission system may cause a reliability problem

on an Affected System.6 SPP, TVA, and MISO are likewise obligated to do the same.

       As Affected Systems of each other, AECI and SPP are parties to a Joint Operating

Agreement (“JOA”), pursuant to which AECI and SPP cooperate on operational, transmission

planning, and other affected system coordination matters (“SPP-AECI JOA”). As relevant here,

the SPP-AECI JOA at Article 7.3 provides in multiple places that the parties will coordinate when

a Party is identified as potentially impacted during studies of generator interconnection and/or

long-term firm transmission service. In relevant part, the parties “will coordinate with respect to

the nature of studies to be performed to test the impacts…on the potentially impacted [p]arty,” and

if the results of the studies indicate an impact, then network upgrades will be identified “in

accordance with procedures, guidelines, criteria, or standards applicable to the potentially

impacted system.”7 While the SPP Tariff’s definition of High Impact Large Load Generation

Assessment (“HILLGA”) includes an evaluation of “the impact of the proposed interconnection

on the safety and reliability of the Transmission System, and, if applicable, an Affected System,” 8

it is unclear from the SPP CHILLS Filing whether CHILLS does. The HILLGA definition notes

that HILLGA is part of the HILL and CHILL processes that study load and generation in

connection with interconnection requests, but there is nothing explicit in the SPP CHILLS Filing

regarding how an Affected System will be identified in the CHILL study process, what the scope

of any such studies may be, or how the study results will factor into transmission service decisions.

As a result, AECI seeks clarification as to whether Affected System Operators will have a formal

role and study rights comparable to those provided for in the SPP Generator Interconnection

Process and the SPP-AECI JOA.

           B.     SPP’s CHILLS Filing Lacks Transparency Regarding Curtailment
                  Procedures and the Mechanism for Physical Control of HILLs by
                  Transmission Operators.

           AECI seeks clarification regarding the concrete steps SPP plans to take to curtail loads

connected via CHILLS in the event there is insufficient transmission capacity to serve these loads.

While the SPP filing explains that CHILLS “is ‘as available’ transmission service that will be

provided by SPP using the transfer capability that is in excess of the capability needed to serve” 9

those customers taking firm service, it is not clear how the actual curtailment process will work.

While SPP explains that it will establish Load Shedding and Curtailment processes in coordination

with the affected Transmission Owner(s) and the Transmission Customer, 10 it does not propose

clear language regarding the mechanics of such coordination with the Affected System. Further,

the filing fails to provide specific details regarding how the curtailment process will be

implemented, whether it will be uniformly applied to CHILLS customers, or how an Affected

System Operator will be able to curtail CHILLS in the event it needs to do so. Instead, SPP vaguely

offers that the affected parties will “implement Load Shedding and Curtailment processes during

any period when SPP determines that such system conditions exist and are necessary to alleviate

said conditions.”11 Rather than deal with curtailment procedures on a case-by-case basis, SPP




9
     SPP CHILLS Filing, Transmittal Letter at 13.
10
     Id. at 28.
11
     Id.
 Docket No. ER26-1323-000
Page 6


should be required to establish a uniform process that is transparent and consistently applied so

that transmission owners and operators understand the actions they are required to take.

        There a several options for SPP to detail the mechanism by which loads taking CHILLS

will be physically curtailed when non-firm transmission service is interrupted. SPP could

document these processes in an Operating Guide, document and implement Reliability

Coordinator or Transmission Operator actions to be taken to effectuate physical curtailments,

establish market-based or flowgate mechanisms, or add a more robustly defined process to the

Tariff. In considering these various approaches, AECI encourages the Commission to direct SPP

to implement a standardized framework that, at a minimum, defines: (i) the events that will trigger

curtailment procedures (e.g., insufficient transmission service or reliability limit violations); (ii)

the roles and responsibilities of SPP, the affected transmission owner(s) and the Transmission

Customer; and (iii) the procedures for coordinating with Affected Systems. AECI notes that in

many instances the affected transmission owner will be the SPP transmission owner directly

serving a load taking CHILLS, rather than an external Affected System. It is therefore important

that the transmission owner serving the load taking CHILLS have meaningful input into the

operating requirements and curtailment criteria, and that the various operational authority and

responsibilities are clearly defined to avoid ambiguity during system events.

        Also problematic, in addition ot the lack of transparency regarding CHILLS, is the fact that

a CHILLS customer can simply pay a penalty if it fails to “fully respond to established Load

Shedding and Curtailment procedures or to cease or reduce service in response to a directive by

SPP.”12 Many of the owners of AI and data center facilities have significant financial backing,


12
     SPP CHILLS Filing, Transmittal Letter at 29.
 Docket No. ER26-1323-000
Page 7


which could undermine any penalty-related incentive for failing to follow curtailment instructions.

For example, the AI company Anthropic recently entered into a $1.5 billion settlement for

unauthorized use of copyrighted material. 13 “But the same week the settlement was first proposed,

Anthropic raised $13 billion at a $183 billion valuation. In effect, Anthropic’s penalty . . .

amounted to less than 1 percent of the company’s total value.” 14 Any fees levied by SPP for a

failure to follow curtailment instructions are likely to have a minimal impact for hyper-scale AI

data centers, thereby undermining the objective of maintaining transmission system reliability

during periods of congestion.

        C.       The Commission Should Direct SPP to Clarify its CHILLS Proposal or
                 Condition Acceptance on SPP Including Tariff Revisions that Ensure Proper
                 CHILLS Implementation.

        Given the issues raised above with respect to the implementation of CHILLS by SPP, the

Commission should require SPP to clarify its plans with respect to engaging with Affected System

Owners and establish concrete procedures for physically curtailing CHILLS. While AECI supports

innovation in transmission service offerings, it believes that emphasizing clear study procedures

and operational frameworks are essential given the scale and characteristics of HILLs. By

requiring SPP to clarify its plans with respect to Affected System Studies and curtailment

procedures at this stage of the process, the Commission will help promote reliable system

operation, reduce implementation-related risks, and provide greater certainty for all stakeholders.

   IV.      CONCLUSION

         WHEREFORE, for the reasons set forth above, AECI respectfully requests that the

Commission grant its motion to intervene and direct SPP to clarify how its CHILLS proposal will

incorporate or build on the Affected System Study process and to provide clear operational

guidance regarding the physical curtailment of CHILLS during transmission system events.
